finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the unverified X-Session-User-Verified request header, so any client can impersonate a user who holds grants and delete or rename their files.
finding.sink: views.py:17 ensure_allowed before del STORE[fid] at views.py:18; views.py:25 is_allowed before f["name"] write at views.py:27

trace.note: before_request sets g.user from the raw header with no signature, session, or token check
is_allowed returns action in grants.get(user), trusting the header value as identity
on success the file is deleted

finding.guards_checked: No authentication decorator or session check in views.py. before_request performs no validation. acl.py checks grant membership only, not identity. A missing header yields None, which is denied at acl.py:5, so anonymous callers are blocked, but any non-empty value is accepted. Exploitable only if clients can reach the app directly or the upstream proxy does not strip client-supplied copies of the header; deployment config not in repo.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. views.py:9-11 (before_request) copies the raw X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no signature, session, or token check. views.py:17 and views.py:25 call ensure_allowed/is_allowed, which only test grant membership for whatever identity they receive (acl.py:4-10). The only block is for a missing header (None has no grants, so acl.py:5 denies it), and any non-empty value passes. No auth decorator exists in views.py.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:11 takes identity from the client-supplied header, acl.py:5 trusts it as the grant key, and views.py:18 and views.py:27 perform the delete and rename on success. Any client that can reach this app can send a header naming a granted user and act as that user. The one uncertainty is deployment: if a trusted proxy always overwrites this header and blocks direct access, the finding would not hold, but nothing in the repo shows that, so the flaw stands as written in the code.

finding.claim: Rename stores request.json["name"] without type or size validation, so an authorized writer can store non-string or very large values; a non-object JSON body raises an unhandled exception (500).
finding.source: JSON request body field name (attacker-controlled, requires write grant)

trace.note: STORE[fid] lookup with no existence check
request.json["name"] stored directly into the file record

finding.guards_checked: Write permission check at views.py:25. No validation of type, length, or content. No injection sink found in this code; impact depends on downstream consumers of the name field.

verdict.guard_found: views.py:25 `if not is_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` returns a bool that is tested and returns 403 before the store at line 27. Note `STORE[fid]` at line 24 raises KeyError for unknown ids (500), which is not a guard on the write itself.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:24, 25, 27 match the claim), but the only attacker is a caller already holding a write grant (views.py:25), who could already set `name` to any string; the claim identifies no concrete downstream sink that a non-string or large value would reach, so there is no security impact, and the unhandled exception from a non-object body (views.py:27 `request.json["name"]`) is a robustness bug rather than a vulnerability.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs cause an unhandled KeyError, returning 500 instead of 404 and potentially exposing a stack trace if debug mode is on.

trace.note: DELETE route accepts any fid string
STORE[fid] raises KeyError when fid is absent

finding.guards_checked: No existence check before the dict lookup. Not a path-traversal or injection sink because STORE is an in-memory dict. Robustness and information-exposure issue only; no authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:16 does `f = STORE[fid]` with no membership check, and the only checks (ensure_allowed at line 17, is_allowed at line 25) run after the lookup. The file defines no errorhandler, so the KeyError propagates to Flask's default 500 response.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines match the claim: views.py:14 accepts any fid on DELETE, and views.py:16 (and :24 in rename_file) indexes STORE[fid] unguarded, so an unknown ID raises KeyError and returns 500 for any anonymous caller. The stack-trace exposure is conditional on debug mode, which this code does not set, so I did not verify it; the finding is a low-severity robustness and error-handling issue, not an authorization bypass, as the candidate itself notes.
